hints: Look carefully at where D sits in the Venn diagram, right in the centre where all three circles for unsaturated triglyceride, haemoglobin and collagen overlap.
Count double bonds in a different way for lipids and proteins. Think C=C in fatty acids, C=O in every peptide bond, plus the many conjugated double bonds in each haem group.
walkthrough:
**Read what D means**

Look at the diagram. D is the middle region shared by all three circles.

So D means a feature found in unsaturated triglyceride AND in haemoglobin AND in collagen.

**Check double bonds in each molecule**

An unsaturated triglyceride has C=C double bonds in its fatty acid tails. One polyunsaturated fatty acid alone can have 2, 3 or more.

Proteins are different. Every peptide bond contains a C=O double bond:
$$peptide\ bond = -CO-NH-\ with\ one\ C=O$$
Both haemoglobin (about 574 amino acids) and collagen (over 1000 amino acids) therefore have hundreds of C=O double bonds. Haemoglobin also has four haem groups, each porphyrin ring has many conjugated C=C and C=N double bonds.

**Conclude the shared feature**

All three molecule types easily have at least four double bonds, just for different chemical reasons.

That is why the correct region is the centre overlap shared by all three, which is D.

options.A: A is only the overlap of unsaturated triglyceride and collagen. It excludes haemoglobin, but haemoglobin also has many double bonds, so this is too narrow.
options.B: B is only the overlap of haemoglobin and collagen. It excludes unsaturated triglyceride, but unsaturated triglycerides also have C=C double bonds, so this is too narrow.
options.C: C is only the overlap of unsaturated triglyceride and haemoglobin. It excludes collagen, but collagen has hundreds of C=O peptide double bonds, so this is too narrow.
options.D: D is the centre shared by all three circles. All three have at least four double bonds from C=C, C=O and haem groups, so this is correct.
